transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE) -- Aisha Khan, Ben Park, Sofia Ruiz, Tom Green (NovaDocs)

Summary:
Quick migration demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together APIs to Redwood API. Covered: request/response mappings, function/tool calling differences, streaming behavior, embeddings parity, rate limits and quotas, security/KMS and VPC options, and pilot/benchmark next steps.

Topics:
- API parity: prompts, completions vs chat, function calling mapping
- Streaming differences and tokenization/counting parity
- Embeddings: dimensional parity and vector norms
- Dedicated/Private deployment considerations (VPC, KMS, SOC2)
- Performance: batching, KV cache, quantization recommendations
- Next steps: parity doc, benchmarks, pilot kickoff

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - im Jamie from Redwood AE, with Luis and Maya on the SE side. how's every one doing?
[00:12] Aisha Khan: Good, thanks. We've been evaluating a couple of vendors and the big ask is parity - we have prod workloads on OpenAI and Anthropic and a chunk on TogetherAI, we want to understand how close Redwood is feature-wise and what hidden gaps we should expect.
[00:25] Luis Ortega: Totally, that's the exact goal for today. we'll run through a parity mapping and show concrete request/response examples, and highlight where runtime differences live - e.g. streaming chunk boundaries, function-calling edge cases, and KV cache semantics.
[00:40] Ben Park: Quick background: our main production flows are chat completions (multi-turn), a lot of function calls for structured outputs, and an embeddings pipeline used for search. Throughput target is 10k qps on embeddings during peak evals, and 200 concurrent chat sessions.
[00:58] Maya Patel: good, that helps us scope. one note up front: when we say parity there are three axes - API shape (requests/responses), model behavior (tokenization, sampling), and infra semantics (timeouts, streaming). we'll flag each example so you can see where subtle diffs happen.
[01:15] Sofia Ruiz: ok, please show examples. also we need to know about credentials and network - we are strict about KMS, HSM keys, and VPC peering for the pilot.
[01:28] Luis Ortega: noted - we'll cover Private/Dedicated options and what we need for network.

[02:02] Luis Ortega: Demo start: first mapping - OpenAI chat call to Redwood chat. here's a sample OpenAI-style request (we paste): role:user content: 'Summarize the meeting', model: 'gpt-4o' etc. In Redwood the call map is extremely similar, we support chat/messages array, but naming for streaming events is slightly different, and token counts reported in responses can be labeled differently.
[02:30] Ben Park: what about function calling? we rely on the openai function calling flow heavily, seems to work but there are malformed edge cases.
[02:37] Luis Ortega: we support function/tool calling. mapping rules: OpenAI "function_call" -> Redwood "tool_call" in our SDKs, but raw REST still accepts the function schema. There is one quirk - our runtime will resolve ambiguous function names by preference order in the tool registry, so if you rely on side-effect ordering you should pin explicit names. sometimes the transcription will say 'toolling' cause of auto-caption but thats just the transcript.
[03:05] Aisha Khan: ok that preference order is important for us - we have 30+ tools registered. can we pin?
[03:10] Luis Ortega: yes you can pin both in the service config and in per-request metadata. We'll put an example in the parity sheet.

[06:00] Jamie Chen: Embeddings mapping: OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small vs Redwood's embedding models - we provide vector dim parity and config for normalization. for search you should be able to swap in the Redwood embedding with minimal changes; however we do recommend running a re-index and a small eval to verify recall drop.
[06:30] Ben Park: what's vector dimension? we use text-embedding-3-small (1536).
[06:34] Maya Patel: Our "rw-embed-sim-lite" is 1536 too for parity. we'll include exact naming in the doc. normalization and cosine vs dot product configs we call out, because sometimes subtle differences change nearest neighbors.

[09:00] Luis Ortega: Token counting: Redwood uses the same tokenizers for major open models but note when you migrate from Anthropic's token counting there can be +/-. Our billing meters tokens on the request and response side similar to OpenAI, we'll share the tokenization examples.
[09:35] Tom Green: security question: do you support customer-managed KMS? and can we integrate HSM?
[09:41] Jamie Chen: Yes - Private and Dedicated both support customer KMS integrations and HSM options via our enterprise path. We'll send the SOC2, ISO, and KMS integration guide after this call.

[12:10] Luis Ortega: Networking: for VPC peering we require a small set of CIDR ranges; for on-prem air-gapped we have an on-prem package. There may be slight differences in TLS ciphers reported by older clients, so we test that during onboarding.

[15:20] Maya Patel: Performance notes: our runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache. For multi-turn chat our KV cache aggressively reuses context to reduce compute. the tradeoff is cold-start latency vs cached path speed. For your 200 concurrent chats we recommend reserved workers (dedicated pool) with autoscale burst up to shared hosted pool.
[16:00] Ben Park: What about quantization? We sometimes run fp16 quantized models using Together's runtime. can Redwood serve Q4_0 quantized variants?
[16:14] Luis Ortega: yes - we support common quantization profiles and recommend a per-workload evaluation. our Optimize toolkit will suggest a quantization profile and batch size to meet latency/cost SLOs. We'll include a suggested config for your chat/eval mix.

[20:05] Jamie Chen: There's also streaming semantics: OpenAI chunks sometimes include incomplete json for function args, Redwood streams stable JSON chunks unless you enable "raw-chunk" mode - but if you rely on partial parsing we can enable a compatible mode. this is one of those subtle diffs.
[20:35] Aisha Khan: great, we parse partial chunks and reassemble; so we'll want the raw-chunk compatibility.

[24:00] Luis Ortega: Demoing the Console quickly - deploy model version pinning, per-route latency budgets, and cost telemetry. shows a route mapped to rw-chat-1 pinned to hardware group gd-pool-2. you can do canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a cheaper model if SLOs are missed.
[25:10] Ben Park: do you expose token-level cost per request in the console?
[25:15] Maya Patel: yes - Console provides token-level breakdowns, per-route cost, and top prompts driving cost. new Optimize recommendations are surfaced there too.

[28:00] Jamie Chen: Questions about quotas/rate-limits - we support per-key quotas and per-route rate limiter. if you need strict deterministic throttle we recommend Dedicated with token bucket config.

[30:00] Tom Green: For procurement, we'll need the SLA, data residency, and a sample contract. can you send that?
[30:08] Jamie Chen: yep. we'll attach standard SLA and enterprise addendum.

[33:00] Luis Ortega: We ran a short throughput demo earlier this week - for embeddings our ML infra uses sharded indexing and batching to reach high throughput. For your 10k qps we usually recommend a small dedicated cluster or a hybrid reserved+hosted approach; the benchmark script will show expected latency p95 at target qps.
[35:10] Ben Park: what's the expected p95 for 10k qps on a typical setup?
[35:17] Luis Ortega: depends on model/quantization. for rw-embed-sim-lite with optimized batching we see p95 sub-20ms for vector compute in our internal runs; end-to-end depends on network and sharding. we'll run a test with your data to be precise.

[38:00] Maya Patel: Notes on failure modes - fallback policies: you can configure automatic fallback to multi-tenant hosted model or a smaller quantized variant when Dedicated capacity is exhausted. This avoids HTTP 5xx spikes.
[39:05] Aisha Khan: that's important - we need predictable behavior on capacity loss.

[41:00] Jamie Chen: Recap: we'll send parity mapping doc, example request/response pairs (OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood), benchmark script, SOC2/KMS docs, and a proposed pilot plan starting 2026-07-21.
[41:25] Ben Park: sounds good. who owns the benchmark run?
[41:30] Luis Ortega: Redwood SEs will run the initial script against a dedicated pilot cluster; we'll invite Ben and the infra folks to watch, and then hand you the script to run in your environment.
[42:00] Sofia Ruiz: can we get a sample contract and pricing estimate for a 6-month pilot?
[42:06] Jamie Chen: yes - i'll follow up with pricing options (hosted vs dedicated) and a pilot SOW.
[43:00] Tom Green: i'll compile our security checklist and share with Jamie and Luis.
[44:00] Jamie Chen: awesome - thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and set the kickoff.

End of transcript.
